source: Khieu Borin, Than Soeurn, Preston T.R. and Sato K. 1996. The role of the sugar palm tree (Borassus flabellifer) in livestock based farming systems in Cambodia. In: Sustainable Livestock Production on Local Feed Resources, FAO Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific (RAP Publication), Bangkok.
text: Sugar palm juice (from Borassus flabellifer, of which Cambodia has an estimated 8 million trees) is a fibre-free, non-competitive energy source for pig feeding that doesn't draw on cereal grain the country already struggles to produce enough of. A study of 105 male and female palm trees over five months found an average juice yield of about 5kg per tree per day (varying 2.7–7.5kg between farmers) with an average sugar content (Brix) of 13.3%; female trees yielded more juice (5.3kg/day) and slightly sweeter juice than male trees (4.7kg/day). The daily juice from just two trees is enough to feed one pig, and the estimated 8 million trees nationally could theoretically support feeding 3–4 million pigs or 14 million ducks.
